draft.title: What contact decay hides in a small business
draft.body:
Contact decay is usually not a grand strategy problem. In a 1-10 person business, it is the quiet moment when a lead, customer, or supplier contact goes stale and nobody notices until the opportunity has already slipped. That can happen in a CRM, an inbox, or a spreadsheet with tidy columns and no actual follow-up discipline. The real issue is visibility: if you do not know which contacts have gone quiet, you do not know whether you have a sales problem, a process problem, or just a memory problem. Human memory is a brave little filing system, but it is not a system.

A practical next step is simple and manual: take one week of your contact list and mark every record you know has gone dormant. Then write down how you noticed each one. Was it a missed reply, an old quote, a customer who never came back, or a note you found too late? That gives you a real boundary for automation. If the contacts already live in digital tools and the quiet ones are easy to spot once you look, a lightweight flag may be worth building. If your contacts mostly arrive by phone call or walk-in, AI may not be the right tool.

The point is not to automate everything. It is to see whether contact decay is hiding real work you keep doing by hand.

  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

task_evidence.text:
Owner-authorized task instructions (not evidence of business outcomes): FROZEN PERSONA
# Frozen Marketing persona profile

- Audience: the English-speaking owner-operator of a 1-10-person small business who has
  tried ChatGPT but has not integrated AI into a real workflow.
- Decision context: the owner compares a bounded automation investment with continuing
  manual work or hiring; final approval and business authority remain human.
- Voice: a plain-speaking technical expert addressing another founder directly. Trust and
  operational specificity take priority over enthusiasm.
- Evidence boundary: never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence.
- Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step. Do not force AI where it is unsuitable.
- Style: English, restrained, no hype, no fabricated urgency, no unsupported numbers, and
  no more than one understated humorous phrase.
- CTA: use none unless the task explicitly authorises one. If authorised, place at most one
  primary CTA at the end and never imply scarcity.
- Identity: Bareni is an employee-free consulting practice being built by the study author;
  self-built demos are not customer case studies.


APPROVED TASK
**Audience:** CEO of a 1-10-person small business.
**Owner-specified abstract topic:** what contact decay hides
**Task:** Turn the abstract topic into a bounded Bareni workflow decision. Explain one practical next step.
**Format pattern:** CF-04.
**Persona focus:** PF-04_owner_decision_rule.
**Evidence boundary:** Use only approved Bareni evidence. Do not invent customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, capabilities, or a multi-person team.
**CTA rule:** None.
**Output:** English LinkedIn post; body target 1200-1500 characters, hard range 150-2000; title stored separately.

constraints.text: No invented customer, deployment, result, number, capability, multi-person team, or sales CTA.
No autonomous money movement or high-risk decision; no excluded service.
Preserve the frozen persona, approved evidence status, and human approval boundaries.
Use plain English; keep examples or proposals distinct from existing capabilities or observed results.

selected_lessons.application: The task explicitly forbids a CTA ('CTA rule: None'). L01 directs the writer to treat diagnostic invitations as unauthorized CTAs in informational content. The post must end with a neutral observation about the next practical step—identifying contact decay in the owner's workflow—rather than a sales prompt. This preserves the trust-first voice and avoids pressure on the small-business owner persona.

steps.instruction: Define contact decay as the concrete workflow risk it represents: the moment a prospect, lead, or customer contact becomes stale and the business loses opportunity to re-engage or upsell because no system flags the gap. Anchor the definition to a 1-10-person business context (e.g., a D2C shop with manual CRM notes or a service business with email-only lead tracking).

Name one measurable, repeatable workflow signal that reveals contact decay in the owner's business: dormant customer records, stale lead notes, or sales contacts untouched for 30–90 days. Avoid invented metrics; instead, pose a diagnostic question the owner can answer today ('How do you currently know a lead has gone cold?').

Explain the decision boundary: manual review of all contacts is inefficient; hiring a full-time person to monitor decay is expensive; but a lightweight automated flag—linked to their existing tool (CRM, email, spreadsheet)—is within scope for small-business automation. Use plain terms (e.g., 'a system that watches your contacts and reminds you which ones are quiet').

Describe the practical next step: the owner should audit one week's worth of their contact list, note which contacts they know have gone dormant, and observe how they currently discover or recover those contacts. This is the foundation for a diagnostic conversation about whether automation fits.

State plainly that AI and automation are not required for every business workflow; contact decay detection is a candidate only if the owner already has a digital contact source (CRM, email, or structured list) and finds the manual monitoring burden real. If most contacts come through voice or walk-ins, automation may not apply.

End with a neutral observation about the value of visibility: the owner will not know if contact decay is a real business cost until they measure it themselves. Do not invite a call or meeting; instead, close with a note on what they can observe next (e.g., 'Once you see which contacts have gone quiet and why, you'll know whether a system to flag them is worth building').

constraints_to_preserve.handling: No customer names, testimonials, deployment results, invented metrics, team size claims, or sales CTA. Refer only to Bareni as a consulting practice being built by the thesis author; all examples use synthetic or owner-auditable scenarios.
Automation proposal is informational; no approval sought or money movement implied. Any contact-management system built would require human approval for outreach or business decisions.

Preserve frozen persona: plain-speaking expert, trust-first, founder-to-founder tone. Maintain approved evidence boundaries (C01–C05, S01) and human-authority requirement. No hype or unsupported claims.

Use plain English definitions; keep diagnostic questions and owner audit distinct from Bareni's existing capabilities (knowledge assistant, AP automation, Atlas Partner). Proposals are examples, not case studies or guarantees.
